opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the core motivations behind why we built Cosmos in the first place.

So if you think about how people have traditionally trained robots or autonomous vehicles, there are two main sources of data. One is real-world data, which is very high fidelity, but it's expensive to collect, it's slow, and for a lot of the most important scenarios, like dangerous edge cases or rare failures, you simply can't collect enough of it, or it would be unsafe to try. The other source is simulation. Simulation is great because it's scalable, it's controllable, you have perfect ground truth labels. But the problem is that simulated worlds don't look and behave exactly like the real world. The lighting is a little off, the textures are too clean, the physics are approximations. And when you train a policy in simulation and deploy it in reality, the model notices that difference, and performance drops. That's what we call the sim-to-real gap.

Cosmos is a world foundation model platform, and the idea is that we pre-train on a very large amount of video data of the real world, so the model learns a lot about how the world looks and how things move and interact. Once you have that, there are several ways it helps close the gap.

The first is what I'd call making simulation look real. You can take the output of a physics simulator, something like Isaac Sim or Omniverse, where you have structured signals like depth, segmentation, edges, and you use a model like Cosmos Transfer to render that into photorealistic video. The physics and the layout come from the simulator, so you keep the control and the ground truth, but the appearance now matches the distribution of real camera data. And you can vary it: change the weather, the time of day, the materials, the lighting, and get a lot of diversity from a single simulated scenario. That's very powerful for data augmentation.

The second is using the world model itself as a kind of learned simulator. Because Cosmos Predict is trained to predict how the future unfolds given the past and possibly an action or a text prompt, you can use it to generate plausible future scenarios, including rare ones. Developers can post-train it on their own robot or their own vehicle data, so it becomes specialized to their embodiment and their environment.

The third is reasoning. With Cosmos Reason, we want a model that understands physical common sense, whether something is physically plausible, what is likely to happen next, so it can act as a critic to filter out bad synthetic data, or help with planning and data curation.

I want to be honest that this doesn't magically eliminate the gap. World models still make mistakes, especially with fine-grained physics like contact and deformable objects, and evaluating them is still an open research problem. But I think the direction is right: instead of choosing between real data that doesn't scale and simulated data that doesn't transfer, you use a foundation model that has absorbed a lot of real-world knowledge as a bridge between them. And because we release Cosmos openly, builders can take it, fine-tune it for their own problem, and hopefully move much faster than if everyone had to build that capability from scratch.

r001.rationale: It describes simulation and real-world differences causing performance to drop, but does not frame the gap as a generalization problem.

r002.rationale: It presents real-world pretraining and synthetic data generation as helpful, but does not identify better data and starting points as more effective current approaches than better environments.

r003.rationale: It discusses predicting future events and physical reasoning, but does not distinguish pattern-based prediction from genuinely understanding physics.

r004.rationale: It says real-world knowledge can bridge the gap, but does not state that a prior capturing physical patterns may help a policy model generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So the core problem for Physical AI is that, unlike language or images, you can't just scrape the internet and get the data you need. A robot or an autonomous vehicle needs to learn from interactions with the physical world, and collecting that data in the real world is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. You can't crash a car ten thousand times to teach it what not to do. So people turn to simulation, but simulation has its own problem, which is the sim-to-real gap. Traditional simulators are built on hand-written physics and hand-authored assets, and the rendered images never quite look like reality, the contacts and dynamics never quite behave like reality. A policy trained there often breaks when you deploy it.

What we're trying to do with Cosmos is attack that gap from the data side. Cosmos is a family of world foundation models, which means models that have learned, from a huge amount of real video, how the physical world looks and how it evolves over time. We trained on millions of hours of driving, robotics, human activity, and so on. Because the model learned from real footage, the worlds it generates inherit the visual and dynamic statistics of reality rather than of a game engine.

In practice there are a few ways builders use this. One is synthetic data generation. If you have a small amount of real robot data, you can ask Cosmos to produce many variations, different lighting, different weather, different objects on the table, different times of day, while keeping the robot's trajectory consistent. That diversity is exactly what makes a policy robust. The second is what we call simulation-to-real augmentation. You take the output of a conventional simulator, which might be a plain, cartoonish render, and Cosmos transforms it into a photorealistic video that respects the original geometry and motion. So you keep the controllability of the simulator but close the appearance gap. The third is using Cosmos as a world model for policy evaluation or planning, where the model predicts what happens next given an action, so you can test a policy against many imagined futures before you ever run it on hardware.

I want to be honest that this does not eliminate the gap entirely. A generative model can still hallucinate physics, and we spend a lot of effort on evaluation and on fine-tuning for specific embodiments. But we open-sourced the models and the data curation pipeline precisely because we think the whole community needs to iterate on this together. Our view is that the bottleneck for Physical AI is data, and world models are the way to manufacture that data at the scale that the next generation of robots will require.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulator mismatch and policies breaking on deployment, but does not frame the gap as a generalization problem.

r002.rationale: It advocates using Cosmos to generate and augment data, but does not compare better data or starting points with improving simulation environments as current approaches.

r003.rationale: It says Cosmos learns how the world looks and evolves and can predict outcomes, and notes possible physics hallucinations; it does not distinguish pattern capture from genuinely understanding physics.

r004.rationale: The response says varied synthetic data can make policies robust, but does not say that a prior capturing physical patterns helps a policy model generalize more easily.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that simulation gives you control, but it doesn’t capture all the complexity of the real world. You can simulate a robot performing a task, but the lighting, the materials, the objects, and their behavior can look quite different when you deploy that robot in a real environment.

Cosmos can help bridge that gap by bringing generative world models into the development process. For example, you can take a structured simulation and generate much richer visual variations around it, while preserving the task you want the robot to learn. That gives builders a way to expose their systems to more diverse conditions without collecting every example in the real world.

The important thing, though, is that realistic-looking video doesn’t automatically mean physically correct behavior. You still need to validate the generated data and test on real hardware. I see Cosmos as a way to make that iteration loop more effective: use simulation for control, world models for diversity, and real-world testing to measure whether you’re actually closing the gap.

r001.rationale: The response describes exposing systems to diverse conditions so they perform better when deployed in differing real environments, framing the gap as a transfer and generalization challenge.

r002.rationale: It proposes using world models to generate visual variations, but does not compare better data or starting points with improving simulation environments.

r003.rationale: It says realistic-looking video may not reflect physically correct behavior, but does not distinguish predicting future events from genuinely understanding physics.

r004.rationale: It discusses generating varied data while preserving the task, but does not say that a prior capturing physical patterns could help a policy model generalize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that simulation gives you control, but it doesn’t always capture the complexity of the real world. You can build a scene, define the physics, and generate training data, but the visual appearance and the diversity of situations can still be limited.

Cosmos can help bridge that gap by taking structured simulation output and generating more realistic, varied video while preserving the underlying scene and action. You could simulate a robot performing a task, then vary the lighting, materials, or surrounding environment. That lets builders expose their models to many more conditions without manually creating every variation or collecting all that data in the real world.

The other opportunity is testing: exploring situations that are rare, expensive, or difficult to reproduce physically. Of course, realistic video alone doesn’t guarantee physically correct behavior. You still need physics simulation and real-world validation. But together, these tools can make the development loop much faster and help builders identify where their systems might fail before deployment.
